experiment_design.technical_details: This study validates the hypothesis that DNA functions as a viable archival storage medium by quantifying its information-theoretic channel capacity. We model the DNA storage system as a discrete memoryless channel (DMC) or a deletion/insertion/substitution channel, incorporating error rates typical of synthesis and sequencing technologies. The core technical task is to derive the Shannon capacity C of this channel under specific biochemical constraints (e.g., homopolymer limits, GC-content balance) and compare it against the theoretical density limits of traditional magnetic tape or optical media. We will implement numerical simulations to estimate mutual information I(X;Y) between input nucleotide sequences and output reads, applying forward error correction (FEC) codes (e.g., Reed-Solomon or LDPC) to determine the net usable capacity.

source.name: Theoretical DNA Storage Channel Models
source.description: Synthetic datasets generated based on error profiles (substitution, insertion, deletion rates) derived from literature cited in EV-Q092-2fbd48e494c76f6214c0e981. Includes parameters for synthesis fidelity and sequencing noise.

target.name: Channel Capacity Bounds and Density Metrics
target.description: Calculated upper bounds on bits per gram and bits per cubic millimeter, alongside channel capacity in bits per symbol, compared against archival benchmarks.

experiment_design.methods: 1. Channel Modeling: Define a probabilistic transition matrix P(Y|X) representing DNA synthesis and sequencing errors, parameterized by empirical error rates from foundational studies. 2. Capacity Estimation: Use the Blahut-Arimoto algorithm or Monte Carlo methods to compute the channel capacity C = max_{P(X)} I(X;Y). 3. Constraint Integration: Impose biological constraints (no long homopolymers, balanced GC content) as input distribution restrictions and recalculate capacity. 4. Benchmarking: Compare the derived theoretical density (bits/gram) against standard archival media (LTO tape, HDD) using established physical constants.

baselines: Unconstrained Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC) with equivalent raw error rate
Standard Magnetic Tape Archival Density (theoretical limit)
Naive DNA Encoding without Error Correction (raw capacity)
experiments.ablation: Varying error rates (synthesis vs. sequencing dominance), removing GC-content constraints, and testing different FEC code rates to observe impact on net capacity.
experiments.validation_protocol: Cross-validate theoretical capacity estimates against published experimental data points from the literature referenced in EV-Q092-2fbd48e494c76f6214c0e981 to ensure model fidelity. Verify that calculated densities exceed minimum archival thresholds (e.g., >10^18 bits/gram).

hypotheses.hypothesis: DNA can function as a viable archival information storage medium because its physical properties support high information density and longevity, as predicted by information-theoretic channel models.
hypotheses.mechanism: The molecular structure of DNA allows for dense encoding of binary data into nucleotide sequences. Information-theoretic frameworks model the DNA storage system as a communication channel with specific capacity limits determined by synthesis/sequencing errors and biochemical constraints, theoretically validating its feasibility for archival purposes despite practical implementation gaps.
hypotheses.falsifiable_prediction: If DNA is a viable storage medium under current theoretical understanding, then established information-theoretic models must demonstrate a non-zero positive channel capacity for DNA storage that exceeds minimum thresholds for archival utility, even when accounting for typical error rates.
required_observations: Derivation or citation of non-zero channel capacity bounds from information-theoretic models of DNA storage
Theoretical comparison of DNA storage density limits against traditional archival media benchmarks
Mathematical proof that error correction is feasible within the derived channel capacity
hypotheses.risk_of_being_wrong: The hypothesis relies on theoretical models which may not account for unmodeled biochemical noise or economic constraints; if the theoretical channel capacity is near-zero under realistic parameters, DNA would not be viable regardless of physical density.

hypotheses.hypothesis: General computational information flow frameworks can be adapted to formally define and quantify the reliability of DNA as an information storage medium, bridging the gap between abstract theory and physical implementation.
hypotheses.mechanism: While DNA has known physical advantages for storage, its operational viability depends on reliable information transfer during write/read cycles. General theoretical frameworks for information flow in computational systems provide formal tools to model these transfers, potentially allowing rigorous definition of DNA storage reliability metrics beyond simple density/longevity claims.
hypotheses.falsifiable_prediction: If general information flow frameworks are applicable to DNA storage, then adapting such a framework to model DNA synthesis/sequencing as a computational process should yield quantifiable reliability metrics (e.g., mutual information bounds) consistent with DNA-specific information-theoretic results.
required_observations: Successful mapping of DNA storage operations onto a general computational information flow framework
Derivation of reliability metrics using the general framework that match or refine DNA-specific theoretical predictions
Demonstration that the general framework captures unique DNA storage constraints (e.g., sequence-dependent errors)
hypotheses.risk_of_being_wrong: General computational frameworks may lack the specificity to capture biochemical nuances of DNA storage, leading to inaccurate or trivial reliability estimates that do not advance beyond existing DNA-specific theories.

experiment_design.technical_details: This study validates the hypothesis that DNA functions as a viable archival storage medium by quantifying its information-theoretic channel capacity. We model the DNA storage system as a discrete memoryless channel (DMC) or a deletion/insertion/substitution channel, incorporating error rates typical of synthesis and sequencing technologies. The core technical task is to derive the Shannon capacity C of this channel under specific biochemical constraints (e.g., homopolymer limits, GC-content balance) and compare it against the theoretical density limits of traditional magnetic tape or optical media. We will implement numerical simulations to estimate mutual information I(X;Y) between input nucleotide sequences and output reads, applying forward error correction (FEC) codes (e.g., Reed-Solomon or LDPC) to determine the net usable capacity.

source.name: Theoretical DNA Storage Channel Models
source.description: Synthetic datasets generated based on error profiles (substitution, insertion, deletion rates) derived from literature cited in EV-Q092-2fbd48e494c76f6214c0e981. Includes parameters for synthesis fidelity and sequencing noise.

target.name: Channel Capacity Bounds and Density Metrics
target.description: Calculated upper bounds on bits per gram and bits per cubic millimeter, alongside channel capacity in bits per symbol, compared against archival benchmarks.

experiment_design.methods: 1. Channel Modeling: Define a probabilistic transition matrix P(Y|X) representing DNA synthesis and sequencing errors, parameterized by empirical error rates from foundational studies. 2. Capacity Estimation: Use the Blahut-Arimoto algorithm or Monte Carlo methods to compute the channel capacity C = max_{P(X)} I(X;Y). 3. Constraint Integration: Impose biological constraints (no long homopolymers, balanced GC content) as input distribution restrictions and recalculate capacity. 4. Benchmarking: Compare the derived theoretical density (bits/gram) against standard archival media (LTO tape, HDD) using established physical constants.

baselines: Unconstrained Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC) with equivalent raw error rate
Standard Magnetic Tape Archival Density (theoretical limit)
Naive DNA Encoding without Error Correction (raw capacity)
experiments.ablation: Varying error rates (synthesis vs. sequencing dominance), removing GC-content constraints, and testing different FEC code rates to observe impact on net capacity.
experiments.validation_protocol: Cross-validate theoretical capacity estimates against published experimental data points from the literature referenced in EV-Q092-2fbd48e494c76f6214c0e981 to ensure model fidelity. Verify that calculated densities exceed minimum archival thresholds (e.g., >10^18 bits/gram).
